front.title: OAuth 2.0 Agent Authorization with Identity Binding and User Consent

abstract.t: This specification defines an extension to the OAuth 2.0 Identity Assertion Grant that adds explicit user consent through a confirmation URL mechanism. Building on the Identity Assertion Grant mechanism, this extension enables secure delegation to autonomous agents while maintaining user control. Unlike the Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628), this flow does not require polling and is designed for AI agents with frontend capabilities. The specification maintains cryptographic binding between user and agent identities in the resulting access token and provides verifiable evidence of user consent.

section.title: Motivation
section.t: AI agents increasingly need to access protected resources on behalf of users. However, existing OAuth 2.0 mechanisms do not adequately address the unique requirements of AI agent authorization:

ul.li: Identity Binding: AI agents operate with their own workload identities (e.g., SPIFFE IDs) distinct from user identities. Current OAuth flows do not provide standardized mechanisms to cryptographically bind user and agent identities in access tokens.

Explicit Consent: Users must understand and approve what operations an AI agent can perform on their behalf. Traditional scope-based authorization is too coarse-grained for AI agent scenarios requiring fine-grained, context-aware policies.

Audit and Accountability: Organizations deploying AI agents need verifiable evidence of user consent for compliance and security purposes. Current OAuth tokens do not include cryptographic evidence of consent.
Cross-Domain Trust: AI agents often operate across organizational boundaries, requiring standardized mechanisms for identity assertion and authorization that work across trust domains.

section.t: This specification addresses these gaps by extending the Identity Assertion Grant with a confirmation URL mechanism that ensures explicit user consent while maintaining strong identity binding between users and agents.

section.title: Requirements Notation
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.title: Terminology
section.t: This specification uses the terms defined in OAuth 2.0 and the Identity Assertion Grant specification .

dl.dd: An autonomous software application acting on behalf of a user. The agent has its own workload identity (e.g., SPIFFE ID) separate from the user's identity.
A URL provided by the authorization server that enables the user to review and approve an authorization request through a browser-based interface.

The cryptographic association between a user's identity and an agent's identity within an access token, ensuring the token represents delegated authority from that specific user to that specific agent.

section.title: Architectural Overview
section.t: This section provides an architectural overview of the agent authorization framework, including design principles, system components, and trust relationships.

section.title: Design Principles
section.t: This specification is guided by the following design principles:

dl.dd: All authorization decisions MUST be based on explicit, verifiable user consent. Cryptographic binding between user and agent identities prevents token substitution attacks.
Users MUST have clear understanding and control over what operations AI agents can perform. Consent interfaces MUST present authorization details in human-readable form.
Access tokens SHOULD remain compact to avoid HTTP header size limitations. Detailed policy and evidence information is available via reference rather than embedded in tokens.
This specification extends existing OAuth 2.0 and Identity Assertion Grant mechanisms without breaking compatibility with standard OAuth deployments.
All authorization decisions MUST be auditable through cryptographically signed evidence records and comprehensive logging.

section.title: System Components
section.t: The agent authorization framework involves the following components:

dl.dd: The resource owner who delegates authorization to an AI agent. The user authenticates with their Identity Provider and provides explicit consent for agent operations.
An autonomous software application that acts on behalf of the user. The agent has its own workload identity (e.g., SPIFFE ID) and initiates authorization requests to access protected resources.
The user's primary identity provider that authenticates the user and issues ID Tokens. The Home IdP is trusted by the user and typically operated by the user's organization or a trusted third party.

The OAuth 2.0 authorization server that validates agent requests, obtains user consent, and issues access tokens with identity binding. The AS operates in the resource domain and may be distinct from the Home IdP.
The server hosting protected resources. The RS validates access tokens, evaluates authorization policies, and enforces access control decisions.

An optional component (e.g., Open Policy Agent) that evaluates authorization policies against request context. The Policy Engine may be integrated with the Resource Server or operate as a separate service.

section.title: Trust Relationships
section.t: The framework establishes the following trust relationships:

ol.li: User → Home IdP: The user trusts their Home IdP to authenticate them and issue valid ID Tokens. This is typically established through account registration and ongoing authentication.
User → Agent: The user trusts the AI agent to act on their behalf within defined boundaries. This trust is established through explicit consent during the authorization flow.
Agent → AS: The agent authenticates to the AS using its workload identity (e.g., SPIFFE ID). The AS validates the agent's identity through attestation or mTLS.
AS → Home IdP: The AS trusts the Home IdP to issue valid ID Tokens for user authentication. This trust is established through OIDC discovery and key validation.
RS → AS: The Resource Server trusts the AS to issue valid access tokens. This trust is established through token signature validation and issuer verification.

section.title: Agent Authorization Grant Type
section.t: This specification extends the Identity Assertion Grant () with a confirmation URL flow. It uses the same grant type value but adds additional request and response parameters. The grant enables an agent to obtain an access token that:

ul.li: Binds the user's identity to the agent's identity;
Reflects explicit user consent for specific operations;
Includes policy-based authorization constraints;
Contains verifiable evidence of user confirmation.

section.title: Relationship to Identity Assertion Grant
section.t: This specification uses the same grant type value as the Identity Assertion Grant: urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:identity-assertion. Implementations MUST support the base ID-JAG specification and this extension. The extension adds optional parameters for policy proposal and introduces a confirmation URL response instead of immediately issuing an access token.

section.title: Protocol Overview
section.t: The following diagram illustrates the complete authorization flow:
The flow consists of the following phases:

ol.li: Authentication: User authenticates with the agent's Identity Provider and receives an ID Token.
Initial Request: Agent submits Identity Assertion Grant request with policy proposal to the Authorization Server.
Session Creation: AS validates request and returns confirmation URL with session identifier.
Consent Redirection: Agent redirects user to AS consent page with CSRF protection (state parameter).
User Consent: User reviews authorization details and approves or denies the request.
Callback: AS redirects user back to agent with authorization code.
Token Exchange: Agent exchanges authorization code for access token.
Token Issuance: AS issues access token with identity binding (user + agent).
API Access: Agent uses access token to access protected resources.
Token Validation: Resource Server validates token signature and claims.
Policy Evaluation: RS evaluates authorization policy using OPA or similar engine.
Authorization Decision: Policy engine returns allow/deny decision.
Response: RS returns API response based on authorization decision.

section.title: Initial Authorization Request
section.t: The agent initiates the flow by submitting an Identity Assertion Grant request to the authorization server's token endpoint, augmented with policy proposal and context parameters:

figure.artwork:
POST /token HTTP/1.1 Host: as.example.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:identity-assertion &assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:assertion-type:id_token &assertion=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJodHRwczovL2lk... &client_id=spiffe://agent.example.com/sha256.abc123... &policy_proposal=eyJ0eXBlIjoicmVnbyIsImNvbnRlbnQiOiJwYWNr... &policy_context=eyJ1c2VyIjp7ImlkIjoidXNlcl8xMjM0NSJ9fQ

section.t: The request parameters are:

dl.dd: REQUIRED. The value urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:identity-assertion as defined in .
REQUIRED. The value urn:ietf:params:oauth:assertion-type:id_token indicating the assertion is an OpenID Connect ID Token.
REQUIRED. A signed ID Token containing the user's identity. The token MUST include the agent's SPIFFE ID in the aud claim to bind the token to the specific agent.
REQUIRED. The agent's identifier, which SHOULD be a SPIFFE ID URI as defined in .
OPTIONAL. A JSON-encoded Rego policy proposal as defined in . When present, this defines the fine-grained operations the agent is requesting authorization for.
OPTIONAL. A JSON object providing context data for policy evaluation, including user identifiers and requested actions.

section.title: Authorization Server Validation
section.t: Upon receiving the request, the authorization server MUST validate:

ol.li: ID Token Signature: Verify the ID Token signature using the issuer's public keys. Validate standard OIDC claims including iss, exp, and nbf.
Audience Binding: Confirm that the aud claim in the ID Token matches the agent's SPIFFE ID provided in client_id. This ensures the ID Token was specifically issued for this agent.
Agent Authentication: Validate the agent's SPIFFE credentials (if using mTLS or attestation-based client authentication).
Policy Syntax: If policy_proposal is present, validate the Rego policy syntax and check for safety properties.

section.t: If validation fails, the authorization server returns an error response as defined in Section 5.2 of .

section.title: Confirmation URL Response
section.t: Upon successful validation, the authorization server does NOT immediately issue an access token. Instead, it creates a pending authorization session and returns a confirmation URL along with a session identifier:
The response parameters are:

dl.dd: REQUIRED. A URL that the agent MUST present to the user for consent. The URL encodes a unique request identifier.
REQUIRED. The lifetime in seconds of the confirmation request (default: 300).
REQUIRED. An opaque identifier for the pending authorization session. The agent uses this value to correlate the initial request with the subsequent callback.
REQUIRED. The lifetime in seconds of the confirmation session (default: 300).

section.t: The authorization server stores the pending authorization state including:

ul.li: The validated ID Token claims (especially sub and aud);
The agent's SPIFFE ID;
The policy proposal (if provided);
A cryptographically random session identifier.

section.t: The confirmation URI MUST be bound to the authenticated agent's identity (via the aud claim in the ID Token) to prevent session hijacking. The URI MUST be single-use and expire after the specified duration.

section.title: User Consent Flow
section.t: The agent redirects the user's browser to the confirmation URI. To prevent CSRF attacks, the agent SHOULD generate a state value and include it in the redirect. The authorization server then presents a consent interface that:

li.t: Authenticates the User (if needed): If the user does not have an active session with the authorization server, prompt for authentication.
Displays Authorization Details: Present human-readable information about what the agent is requesting:

ul.li: Agent identity (name, organization);
Requested operations (derived from policy proposal);
Resource server being accessed;
Duration of authorization.

li.t: Presents Consent Options: Allow the user to approve or deny the request.

section.title: Consent Page Example

figure.artwork: +----------------------------------------------------------+ | Authorize Agent Access | +----------------------------------------------------------+ | | | Agent: MyShopping Assistant (myassistant.example.com) | | | | This agent is requesting permission to: | | | | - Add items to your shopping cart (max $50 per item) | | - View product recommendations | | - Update shipping address | | | | Resource Server: Shop Example (shop.example.com) | | | | Duration: Until you revoke access | | | | +------------------+ +------------------+ | | | Allow | | Deny | | | +------------------+ +------------------+ | | | +----------------------------------------------------------+

section.t: The authorization server is responsible for interpreting the policy proposal and presenting it in human-readable form. The example above shows how a Rego policy might be translated into user-friendly language.

section.title: Policy Interpretation
section.t: Authorization servers MUST interpret policy proposals and present them to users in a clear, understandable manner. The following guidelines apply:

section.title: Interpretation Requirements
section.t: The consent interface MUST display:

ul.li: Agent Identity: The name and identifier of the AI agent requesting authorization, verified through its authenticated workload identity.
Requested Operations: A human-readable summary of the operations the agent is requesting permission to perform, derived from the policy proposal.
Constraints and Limitations: Any constraints specified in the policy (e.g., monetary limits, time restrictions, resource scopes).
Resource Server: The target resource server or service that the agent will access.
Authorization Duration: The lifetime of the authorization and conditions for renewal or revocation.

section.title: Best Practices
section.t: Authorization servers SHOULD follow these best practices for policy interpretation:

ul.li: Use clear, non-technical language that average users can understand;
Highlight high-risk operations (e.g., financial transactions, data deletion) with appropriate warnings;
Provide expandable sections for users who want to see technical details of the policy;
Include examples of what the agent can and cannot do with the requested authorization;
Support multiple languages and accessibility features (screen readers, high contrast modes);
Allow users to selectively approve or deny specific operations if the policy permits granular consent.

section.title: User Confirmation Action
section.t: When the user clicks "Allow", the authorization server:

li.t: Records the user's consent with a timestamp;
Redirects the user's browser back to the agent's redirect URI with the authorization code and state parameter:

section.t: The state parameter MUST match the value provided in the redirect to the confirmation URI. The agent MUST validate the state parameter to prevent CSRF attacks.

section.title: Token Request
section.t: After receiving the authorization code, the agent exchanges it for an access token:

figure.artwork:
POST /token HTTP/1.1 Host: as.example.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Authorization: Basic czZCaGRSa3F0MzpnWDFmQmF0M2JW
grant_type=authorization_code &code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA &redirect_uri=https://agent.example.com/callback

section.t: The authorization server validates:

ul.li: The authorization code is valid and unexpired;
The redirect_uri matches the registered URI;
The agent's client credentials are valid.

section.title: Access Token Response
section.t: Upon successful validation, the authorization server issues an access token with identity binding:
The JWT access token contains the following claims:

dl.dd: The authorization server's identifier.
The user's identifier at the resource server (extracted from ID Token).
The resource server's identifier.

li.t: sub: The agent's SPIFFE ID (from client_id);
agent_user_id (OPTIONAL): The user's identifier at the agent system.

dl.dd: OPTIONAL. A JSON string containing a policy identifier, or a JSON array of strings when multiple policies apply. The resource server can fetch the full policy content from the endpoint specified in the authorization server's metadata or via token introspection.
OPTIONAL. A JSON string containing an evidence identifier referencing the user consent record. The full evidence details can be retrieved via token introspection.

OPTIONAL. If present, the refresh token MUST contain the same identity binding as the access token (i.e., the same act claim). When used to obtain a new access token, the resulting token MUST maintain the same user-agent binding unless the user explicitly re-authenticates.

REQUIRED. The expiration time of the access token. For AI agent scenarios, short-lived tokens (e.g., 1 hour) are RECOMMENDED to limit the window of exposure if a token is compromised. Longer durations MAY be used when combined with strong binding and continuous authentication mechanisms.

section.t: The full policy content and evidence details are available via token introspection or from the policy endpoint. This design keeps the token compact while enabling detailed verification when needed.

section.title: Token Lifetime Recommendations
section.t: Authorization servers SHOULD follow these token lifetime guidelines:

Authorization servers MAY adjust these values based on risk assessment, user authentication strength, and operational requirements. Tokens issued for high-risk operations (e.g., financial transactions) SHOULD have shorter lifetimes.

section.title: Token Introspection Response
section.t: When a resource server performs token introspection , the authorization server MAY return additional claims beyond the standard OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection response:
The introspection response includes:

dl.dd: OPTIONAL. The full policy content referenced by policy_ref. This enables resource servers to evaluate policies without additional round-trips to the policy endpoint.
OPTIONAL. The complete evidence record referenced by evidence_ref. Includes user confirmation details and authorization server signature for audit purposes.

section.t: Authorization servers SHOULD support token introspection for agent authorization tokens to enable resource servers to obtain complete authorization context. However, implementations MAY choose to omit policy_content and evidence_details from introspection responses for privacy or performance reasons, requiring resource servers to fetch this information separately from the policy and evidence endpoints.

section.title: Threat Model
section.t: This specification addresses the following threats specific to AI agent authorization:

tr.td: Audience binding (ID Token aud == agent SPIFFE ID)
Bind confirmation request to authenticated agent session
Explicit user consent required via secure UI
One-time authorization codes with short expiry

section.title: Trust Boundaries
section.t: The framework establishes clear trust boundaries:

ul.li: User → Agent: ID Token with agent in audience (binds user to agent);
Agent → AS: SPIFFE authentication + ID Token assertion;
AS → User: Secure consent interface (HTTPS);
AS → Agent: Signed access token with identity binding;
Agent → RS: Access token with policy reference and evidence.

section.title: Consent Security
section.t: The consent process MUST be secured:

ul.li: Confirmation URLs MUST be served over HTTPS and MUST NOT be sent over unencrypted channels;
Confirmation URLs MUST be bound to the authenticated agent's identity (e.g., via mTLS or DPoP) to prevent hijacking;
Confirmation URLs MUST be single-use and expire within 5 minutes;
Authorization codes MUST be single-use and expire quickly (recommended: 10 minutes);
State parameter MUST be used and validated to prevent CSRF attacks;
Evidence records SHOULD be made available via token introspection for audit purposes.

section.title: Difference from Device Authorization Grant
section.t: This specification is sometimes confused with the Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628). While both flows involve separated user interaction, they address different use cases:

dl.dd: Designed for input-constrained devices (TVs, IoT) that cannot render browsers. Requires polling the token endpoint waiting for user approval. User enters a code on a separate device.

Designed for AI agents with frontend capabilities. No polling required - uses standard OAuth redirect callback. User is redirected to authorization server's consent page directly from the agent's interface.

section.t: Key differences:

ul.li: No polling: Agent receives confirmation URL immediately;
No user codes: Standard OAuth redirect with authorization code;
Faster completion: Real-time redirect vs. polling interval delays;
Better UX: Seamless integration with agent's frontend.

section.title: Confirmation URL Binding
section.t: The authorization server MUST bind the confirmation URL to the authenticated agent's identity. When the user completes consent, the AS MUST verify that the entity completing consent matches the original requester identified in the ID Token's aud claim.
This prevents an attacker from intercepting a confirmation URL and substituting their own identity during the consent flow (token confusion attack).

section.title: Token Revocation
Revocation Triggers
section.t: Authorization servers SHOULD revoke agent authorization tokens in the following situations:

ul.li: User explicitly revokes authorization for the agent;
Agent's workload identity is compromised or rotated;
Policy associated with the token is updated or deprecated;
User's account is suspended or terminated;
Anomalous activity is detected indicating potential token misuse.

section.title: Revocation Propagation
section.t: When an access token is revoked, the authorization server SHOULD also revoke associated artifacts:

ul.li: The refresh token used to obtain the access token;
Other access tokens issued with the same user-agent binding;
Pending confirmation sessions for the same agent.

section.t: Resource servers SHOULD check token revocation status through token introspection or by maintaining a local revocation cache. The cache SHOULD be updated frequently (e.g., every 5 minutes) to balance performance with security requirements.

section.title: Revocation Evidence
section.t: Authorization servers SHOULD maintain evidence of token revocation for audit purposes. The evidence SHOULD include:

ul.li: Token identifier (jti claim);
Revocation timestamp;
Reason for revocation;
Entity that initiated revocation (user, admin, system);
Notification status (if user was notified).

section.title: Privacy Considerations
section.t: This specification involves processing of user identity information across trust domains. Implementers SHOULD consider the following privacy implications:

section.title: Identifier Minimization
section.t: Agents SHOULD minimize exposure of user identifiers. The sub claim in access tokens SHOULD use pairwise pseudonymous identifiers as described in to prevent correlation across different resource servers.

section.title: Evidence Retention
section.t: Authorization servers SHOULD limit retention periods for evidence records. Once the access token expires, the detailed evidence MAY be deleted while maintaining minimal audit logs for security purposes.

section.title: Logging Considerations
section.t: Authorization servers SHOULD NOT log full ID Tokens or complete evidence records. Logs SHOULD contain only minimal identifiers necessary for security monitoring and debugging.

section.title: Error Handling
section.t: This specification extends the error codes defined in Section 5.2 of with the following values:

dl.dd: The policy_proposal parameter contains malformed Rego policy. The error response SHOULD include a human-readable description of the syntax error.
The confirmation URL has expired (typically after 5 minutes). The agent MUST restart the authorization flow.
The user explicitly denied consent. The authorization server MAY provide this information to the agent via error response or silent callback.
The session identifier in the confirmation URL is invalid or has already been used. This MAY indicate a replay attack attempt.

section.title: Implementation Considerations
section.t: This section provides guidance for implementers of the agent authorization framework, including deployment patterns, performance considerations, and interoperability guidelines.

section.title: Deployment Patterns
section.t: The agent authorization framework supports several deployment patterns:

dl.dd: The Home IdP, Authorization Server, and Resource Server are all operated by the same organization. This simplifies trust establishment but limits cross-organizational agent usage.
The Home IdP is operated by the user's organization, while the AS and RS are operated by a resource provider. This requires cross-domain trust establishment through OIDC federation.
Multiple AI agents from different vendors access resources on behalf of the same user. Each agent has its own workload identity and may access different resource servers.
An AI agent delegates authorization to a sub-agent (e.g., a specialized service agent). This requires support for delegation chains.

section.title: Performance Considerations
section.t: Implementers SHOULD consider the following performance factors:

ul.li: Token Introspection Caching: Resource servers SHOULD cache introspection responses to reduce load on the authorization server. Cache duration should balance performance with security requirements.
Policy Evaluation: Complex Rego policies may introduce latency. Resource servers SHOULD cache policy evaluation results when appropriate.
Confirmation Session Storage: Authorization servers SHOULD use distributed session storage (e.g., Redis, memcached) for confirmation sessions to support horizontal scaling.
Evidence Record Storage: Evidence records may accumulate rapidly. Implementers SHOULD establish retention policies and archival strategies.

section.title: Interoperability Guidelines
section.t: To ensure interoperability between different implementations:

ul.li: Implementations MUST support the mandatory features defined in this specification;
Implementations SHOULD support token introspection for complete authorization context;
Implementations MAY support optional features (e.g., policy content in introspection responses) with graceful degradation;
Implementations SHOULD publish their supported features in authorization server metadata;
Implementations MUST handle unknown claims gracefully without failing.

section.title: ABNF Syntax
section.t: This specification uses the Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) notation defined in . The following terms are defined for use in this specification:

figure.artwork:
grant-type = "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:identity-assertion" assertion-type = "urn:ietf:params:oauth:assertion-type:id_token"
policy-proposal = "policy_proposal" "=" policy-json policy-json = 1*( %x20-21 / %x23-7B / %x7D-7E )
policy-context = "policy_context" "=" context-json context-json = 1*( %x20-21 / %x23-7B / %x7D-7E )
confirmation-uri = "confirmation_uri" "=" uri session-id = "session_id" "=" 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" ) state-param = "state" "=" 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "_" / "." )
error-code = "invalid_policy_syntax" / "confirmation_expired" / "user_denied_consent" / "session_not_found"

section.title: IANA Considerations
section.t: This specification extends the Identity Assertion Grant with additional parameters and token claims. No new grant type is registered since this specification uses the existing urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:identity-assertion grant type defined in .

section.title: JWT Claim Registration
section.t: This specification registers the following claims in the JSON Web Token Claims registry ():

dl.dd: Reference to authorized policy/policies
IETF
[This document]
Reference to user consent evidence record
IETF
[This document]

section.t: Note: Full policy content and evidence details are available via token introspection rather than embedded in the token to minimize token size.

section.title: Authorization Server Metadata
section.t: An authorization server supporting this specification SHOULD include the following parameters in its OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata document :

dl.dd: URL of the confirmation page used for user consent. This endpoint accepts HTTP GET requests with a session identifier parameter.
URL template for retrieving policy content by policy ID. The template MUST contain the placeholder {policy_id}.
URL template for retrieving evidence content by evidence ID. The template MUST contain the placeholder {evidence_id}.
